blockers.quote: A typical worker across the river makes about nine dollars a day (c22). Now they cross to sleep.
blockers.why: Claim c22 is explicitly based on 2019 figures from ProPublica. Stating in present tense that a worker makes about nine dollars a day violates scope rules by stating a 2019 period finding as a general present-day fact.
blockers.fix: In 2019, a typical worker across the river made about nine dollars a day (c22). Now they cross to sleep.

blockers.quote: Twice a week, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows (c02).
blockers.why: Claim c02's verbatim quote from 21 CFR 640.65(b)(8) specifies donations cannot occur 'more frequently than twice in a 7-day period' and must 'not occur less than 2 days apart'. Stating 'Twice a week... It's the most the law allows' overstates the regulatory limit by omitting the rolling 7-day window and 2-day minimum interval.
blockers.fix: Twice in seven days, you sell your plasma, the pale part of your blood. It's the most the law allows (c02).

blockers.quote: Your brain needs that night shift to file your day. For a month, nothing's been filed.
blockers.why: States as a real-world biological fact that the human brain requires sleep to file memories, but cites no claim row. Claim c14 is strictly scoped to animal recording in rats, and human memory study c13 was dropped in v5.

keep.quote: It's true. In 2022, brain cells in a dish, wired to the old bat-and-ball video game, began to get better at it within five minutes (c19). So a whole brain for eight hours is a bargain.
In mice, the spaces between brain cells open up by about sixty per cent during sleep, and the waste washes out faster (c12). Sleep is when your brain takes the trash out. Yours hasn't in a month.

So is a sleeping brain really working? About a hundred years ago a scientist said the experiment that won him a Nobel Prize came to him in a dream. He got up in the night and did it, on a frog's heart (c21).
